name: Zillow's Zestimate page: how its home valuation model works
title: Zillow's Zestimate page: how its home valuation model works
answer: This is Zillow's own explainer page for the Zestimate, its automated home valuation. It describes a neural network based model that draws on public records, MLS feeds and user submitted details to value more than 120 million homes, published free as a starting point rather than an appraisal. The most useful point for anyone watching production machine learning is that Zillow states the model is applied uniformly across homes and that estimates update several times a week, with an estimated sales range published alongside each single value.

sections.body: Zillow publishes this page on zillow.com as a consumer explainer for the Zestimate, its automated estimate of a home's market value. It covers what the Zestimate is, which data feeds it, how often it updates, why some homes do not have one and how the model has changed over time. It is first party vendor documentation rather than an independent study, and the page states no publication or revision date. The only dating in the text is a reference to Zillow being founded in 2006 and to nearly 20 years of model development.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The Zestimate is Zillow's estimate of a home's market value, built from public records, MLS data and user submitted home details. Zillow calls it a transparent, free starting point for homeowners, buyers and sellers, and states it is not an appraisal and cannot replace one. Zillow publishes Zestimates for more than 120 million homes and says the models are statistical and machine learning based, analysing hundreds of data points per property. The calculation uses a neural network based model drawing on county and tax assessor records and direct MLS feeds. Alongside each value Zillow publishes an estimated sales range, which it says captures uncertainty from negotiation and changing market conditions, with the Zestimate representing the most likely outcome. The latest model uses an updated neural network architecture and expanded historical data, which Zillow says improved accuracy for on-market and off-market homes and reduced overall error rates. For on-market homes the model also uses listing information such as list price and recent market activity, which is unavailable off-market, so an estimate may shift once a listing goes live. Most Zestimates update multiple times per week. Updates to home facts are incorporated, though cosmetic changes may not move the value. Zillow says the model is applied uniformly across homes using standardized data such as bedroom and bathroom counts, square footage, lot size, tax assessments and prior sales.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Zillow states that it publishes Zestimates for more than 120 million homes and that it has data on more than 125 million homes, publishing estimates for most of them. It says the model analyses hundreds of data points per property, that most Zestimates update multiple times per week, and that Zillow was founded in 2006 and has spent nearly 20 years developing the model. It gives no error rate or accuracy figure on this page. Other positions stated: the Zestimate is not an appraisal, it is a neutral estimate applied uniformly across homes, and a missing Zestimate usually means insufficient reliable data, incomplete or inconsistent property information, an estimate the model judges too uncertain, or limited recent sales activity.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in real estate can use this page to see how a large scale automated valuation model is described by the company that runs it: which data feeds it, how listing signals change an estimate, how uncertainty is published as a range rather than a single number, and why coverage is deliberately incomplete when data is thin. It is a first party account of a production machine learning system serving consumers at national scale, useful for understanding the design choices and the vocabulary, such as on-market versus off-market inputs, that appear across the sector.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: The page is Zillow's own explainer, so every claim is self reported and no independent validation is offered. It gives no error rate, no accuracy percentage and no methodology detail beyond naming a neural network architecture and listing data sources. It does not compare the Zestimate with other valuation models, does not discuss regulation or liability, and states no publication or revision date. It is a consumer facing page rather than a technical paper, so a reader wanting measured performance would need to look elsewhere.
